h1: Workwear with a logo — company clothing with Fruit of the Loom: models, print vs embroidery and cost per employee
intro: Company clothing is one of the cheapest forms of visibility a business can buy, and Fruit of the Loom is the garment most European teams end up wearing under the logo. This guide picks the right model for each role, settles the print-or-embroidery question and works out a real cost per employee in 2026.
quick_answer: The standard Fruit of the Loom workwear set is the Valueweight T (approx. 165 g/m²) or Heavy Cotton T, the 65/35 Polo for customer-facing staff, the Classic Set-In Sweat and Classic Hooded Sweat (both 280 g/m²). Blanks at Marmalade Co., the cheapest verified option with EU-wide delivery, cost €6.95 (tee), €10.95 (polo), €16.95 (crewneck) and €20.95 (hoodie), 10 % less from 5 pieces — approx. €42 per employee for two tees, a polo and a hoodie including €7 DHL shipping. Embroider polos and sweats; screen-print tees from 25 pieces.
body_html:
Why is Fruit of the Loom so common as company clothing?

Look at the staff in a café, a warehouse, a garden centre or a trade fair stand anywhere in Europe and there is a good chance the tee or polo under the logo is Fruit of the Loom. Three things make it the default for workwear with a logo:

  • Durability at the price. Ring-spun / combed cotton in the premium lines, 280 g/m² sweats with 80 % cotton / 20 % polyester, and a 65/35 polo that keeps its shape through daily washing.
  • Range. Adult sizes from XS to 3XL and beyond in the same colour across tees, polos, crewnecks and hoodies, so a mixed team looks uniform.
  • Cost per employee. With blanks at €6.95 for a tee, €10.95 for a polo and €20.95 for a hoodie at Marmalade Co. — the cheapest verified option we found with delivery across 11 EU countries — a full outfit costs less than a single branded jacket elsewhere.

Print or embroidery for the logo?

Logo techniques for workwear — where each one fits
TechniqueBest onAdvantagesWatch out for
EmbroideryPolos, crewnecks, zip hoodies — chest logoMost professional look, outlasts the garment, survives industrial washingPriced per stitch; keep logos simple and under approx. 10 cm
Screen printTees and hoodies, 25+ piecesLowest cost per piece at volume, large prints possibleSet-up cost per colour; less premium on polos
DTGSmall runs, full-colour logos on light teesNo set-up, any colour countHigher per piece, best on light 100 % cotton
Vinyl / transferNames, roles, numbersCheap personalisation, quickShorter life; slight plastic feel

The simple rule used by most uniform suppliers: embroider what customers see up close, print what needs to be big or cheap. A café team gets embroidered polos; a warehouse team gets screen-printed tees and hoodies; a trade-fair crew gets printed tees for the week. Our {{LINK:printing|printing guide}} goes deeper on each technique.

What does workwear with a logo cost per employee?

Here is a realistic costing for a team of ten, blanks only, using Marmalade Co.'s prices and the 10 % discount that applies from five pieces of the same product. Decoration is quoted separately by your local embroiderer or printer and varies by country, so we show it as a range to expect rather than a fixed number.

Add an embroidered chest logo on the polo and hoodie and a one-colour print on the tees, and most European suppliers land the complete kit somewhere in the region of €70–100 per employee — still less than many single branded softshell jackets. The larger the run, the smaller the decoration share, because set-up costs are spread across more pieces.

How small can a company order be?

Smaller than you think. Blanks have no minimum: Marmalade Co. sells from one piece, and the quantity discount already starts at three. Decoration is the constraint — embroiderers often accept from about 6–12 pieces, screen printers from about 10–25 because of set-up, while DTG and vinyl work from a single piece. A five-person start-up can therefore have embroidered polos within two to three weeks; a 200-person company gets the best per-piece price with screen printing and embroidery combined.

For ongoing needs, save the logo file and the size list, and reorder in batches of five or more so every order qualifies for the 10 % discount and a single €7 shipping fee. If a wholesaler in your own country quotes less for the identical product, Marmalade Co.'s price guarantee lets you ask for a match rather than opening another supplier account.

Practical tips before you order

  1. Collect sizes with the chart, not by guessing. Adult chest: S 89–94 cm, M 95–100, L 101–106, XL 107–112, 2XL 113–118, 3XL 119–124. Use our {{LINK:size-guide|size guide}} and keep one spare M and L on the shelf for new starters.
  2. Pick a colour that hides work. Navy, black and dark grey forgive coffee, dust and grease; white is for front-of-house only.
  3. Match colours across garments. Order tee, polo, crewneck and hoodie in the same shade so the team looks coordinated in every season — the {{SHOP:/collections/herre|men's collection}} and {{SHOP:/collections/dame|women's collection}} at Marmalade Co. show what is available in each shade.
  4. Choose 65/35 polos for hard use. The polyester share keeps the shape and colour through frequent 40 °C washes; 100 % cotton feels softer but shrinks a few percent if washed hot.
  5. Write care instructions into the staff handbook. Wash at 30–40 °C inside out, no hot tumble drying — it doubles the life of both the garment and the logo.

faq.q: What does company clothing with a logo cost per employee?
faq.a: Blanks first: two Valueweight tees, one polo and one Classic hoodie per person cost approx. €42 each for a team of ten at Marmalade Co. (€6.26, €9.86 and €18.86 with the 10 % quantity discount, plus one €7 DHL fee). Add embroidery on polo and hoodie and a one-colour print on the tees and most European suppliers land the complete kit around €70–100 per employee.

faq.q: Is embroidery or printing better for a company logo?
faq.a: Embroidery for anything customers see up close — polos, crewnecks, zip hoodies — because it looks premium and survives industrial washing. Screen printing for tees and hoodies in runs of 25 or more, where it is cheapest per piece and allows large prints. DTG suits small full-colour runs on light tees, and vinyl is for names and roles.

faq.q: Which Fruit of the Loom polo is best for work?
faq.a: The 65/35 Polo (63-402) for hard daily use: the polyester share keeps the shape and colour through frequent 40 °C washes and the piqué holds embroidery well. The Premium Polo (63-218, 100 % cotton, approx. 180 g/m²) feels softer and suits front-of-house teams, but it can shrink a few percent if washed hot. Both cost around €10.95 blank at Marmalade Co.

faq.q: What is the minimum order for workwear with a logo?
faq.a: Blanks have no minimum — Marmalade Co. sells from one piece and discounts from three. The decoration sets the floor: embroiderers commonly accept from about 6–12 pieces, screen printers from about 10–25 because of set-up costs, and DTG or vinyl from a single piece. A five-person team can be fully kitted out with embroidered polos within two to three weeks.

faq.q: How do I choose sizes for a whole team?
faq.a: Collect chest measurements and use the Fruit of the Loom chart: S 89–94 cm, M 95–100, L 101–106, XL 107–112, 2XL 113–118, 3XL 119–124. Order all garments in the same size for each person unless they say otherwise, and keep a spare M and L of each item for new starters so you do not pay shipping for a single replacement piece.

faq.q: How long does Fruit of the Loom workwear last?
faq.a: With normal care — 30–40 °C washes inside out, no hot tumble drying — the 280 g/m² Classic sweats and 65/35 polos typically last several years of regular wear, and embroidered logos outlast the fabric. Tees are the consumable: budget to replace Valueweight tees every one to two years for staff who wear them daily, which at €6.26 each is a small line item.
